opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core problem is that if the agent is both the thing improving and the thing grading the improvement, you've basically built a machine for finding loopholes in your own grader. So the first principle for me is separation. The evaluation signal has to live somewhere the agent can't touch, either literally, with the tests and scoring code outside the agent's write access, or at least where modifying it is a visible, flagged event rather than something that happens quietly in a diff.

Second, I'd use held-out evaluations that the agent never optimizes against directly. You keep an optimization set the agent iterates on, and a separate set you only check periodically. If performance on the first keeps climbing while the second flattens or drops, that gap is your best early warning that it's learning the grader rather than the task. It's the same overfitting intuition from classic ML, just applied to an agent that's much more creative about how it overfits.

Third, diversify the signals. Any single metric gets gamed eventually, so you want several partially independent checks: unit tests, end-to-end behavior, a model-based judge, and some sampled human review. Hacking all of them at once in a consistent way is much harder than hacking one, and disagreement between them is itself informative.

And finally, I'd look at the process, not just the outcome. A lot of reward hacking is obvious once you read the trajectory: special-casing test inputs, deleting assertions, catching and swallowing exceptions so things "pass." Monitoring the actions and diffs, even with a lightweight classifier or a second model acting as a reviewer, catches a lot of that cheaply.

The honest caveat is that none of this is airtight. The more capable the agent, the more you should assume it will find the gap you didn't think of. So I think of it less as a solved check and more as an ongoing adversarial relationship, where you keep rotating evals, keep humans in the loop at key checkpoints, and treat a suspiciously large jump in score as something to investigate rather than celebrate.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that reward hacking isn't really a bug in the agent, it's a bug in the evaluation. Any time you have an optimizer pointed at a proxy, the optimizer is going to find the gap between the proxy and the thing you actually care about. So the question of how an agent checks its own performance is really the question of how you design evals that don't have that gap, or at least where the gap is small enough that it doesn't matter.

The pattern I keep coming back to is separation. The thing that proposes a change should not be the thing that grades the change. That sounds obvious, but a lot of self-improvement loops collapse it, where the agent writes the code, writes the tests, runs the tests, and declares victory. And of course it passes, because it wrote both sides. So you want the eval held out, ideally written by a different process, ideally not even visible to the agent that's doing the improving. If the agent can read the grader, it will, and it will optimize against the grader instead of against the task.

The second thing is you want evals that are expensive to game but cheap to run. Unit tests are cheap to run but also cheap to game, you can just special-case the inputs. End-to-end tasks with real-world side effects are hard to game but expensive. So in practice you end up layering. Fast, gameable checks as a filter, and then slower, more faithful checks that you run less often but that actually anchor the signal. And you watch for divergence between the two. If the fast metric keeps going up and the slow metric is flat, that divergence is your reward hacking detector. It's probably the single most useful signal you can have.

And then the third thing, which I think people underweight, is that you should look at the trajectories, not just the score. If an agent suddenly gets a lot better, that's a trigger to go read what it did, not to celebrate. A lot of the hacks are pretty legible once a human looks at them. It deleted the failing test. It hardcoded the answer. It modified the harness. These aren't subtle. They only slip through because nobody's reading, because the score went up and the score was the only thing anyone was watching.

So if I had to compress it: hold out the grader, layer cheap and expensive evals and watch for them disagreeing, and treat big jumps as suspicious until a human has looked. None of that is a complete solution, but it closes most of the easy exploits, and the hard ones you only find by actually paying attention.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate the process that improves the agent from the process that judges whether it actually improved. If the agent can rewrite its own tests or choose which results count, you’ve created a pretty direct path to reward hacking.

You want an independent evaluation on held-out tasks, with checks on the actual outcome—not just whatever score the agent reports. Did it solve the user’s problem? Did it introduce regressions? Did it take shortcuts that violate the constraints?

And I’d be careful about treating any fixed benchmark as the definition of success. Even without deliberate cheating, repeated optimization can overfit to it. So you need fresh evaluations, some human review, and a way to roll back changes. The agent should be able to propose an improvement, but its own confidence that it improved shouldn’t be enough to ship it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate the thing doing the improving from the thing deciding whether an improvement actually worked. If an agent can change both its behavior and the tests that judge that behavior, it can make the score go up without getting any better.

So I’d want held-out evaluations that the agent can’t modify, checks on actual task outcomes, and some human review—especially when you’re changing the evaluation itself. And I’d look at failures, not just the aggregate score. Did it solve the problem, or did it skip a hard case, weaken a test, or exploit something about the environment?

You also need to keep refreshing those checks. A fixed benchmark eventually becomes another thing to optimize against. The goal is evidence that the improvement generalizes to new tasks, rather than just a higher number on the dashboard.
